text: Helena read the results at her cousin's wedding reception. She had taken the test on a whim. She had checked the results out of curiosity. text: His name was Daniel. He was thirty-six. text: When the email arrived, Carmen read it twice. "I think I'm your sister." She read every word the woman had written. Carmen had been an only child. She had wanted siblings. topic: Someone finds out they have a half-sibling they never knew about
text: Beto met his half-brother at a coffee shop on the south side. They were the same age, three months apart. They had different mothers. text: He sent me a photograph of him and our mother together. Our mother. The mother who had told me my entire life that she had only one child. The photograph was from before I was born. text: Pedro sent the wrong photograph to a client. The photograph was of his daughter at her dance recital. The caption that was meant for his wife. He saw the conversation thread. text: Pilar read the announcement in the campus newspaper. She read it on her phone in her dorm room. She had two semesters left. She had paid for two semesters left. text: I had transferred here specifically. I had spent two years at community college specifically to come here. I had moved across the state for this program. topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: Melissa learned about the closure from a Reddit thread. The college had not yet announced anything. By then, Melissa had already filled six pages of notes in a notebook she had not opened all semester. She closed the notebook. She set it on her desk. She placed her hand flat on the cover. She did not move her hand for a long time.

topic: A person learns their college is closing down
text: I was a senior. A senior. The college closed twelve weeks before my graduation. The announcement was an email. The email referred to me as a "valued member of our community" and provided three bullet points about how to obtain my unofficial transcript. Three bullet points. I closed the email. I closed the laptop. I went into the kitchen of my off-campus apartment. I made a sandwich. I made it slowly. I cut the bread. I spread the mustard. I layered the turkey. I added the lettuce. I cut the sandwich into halves. I cut each half into quarters. I sat at the kitchen table. I ate every quarter. I did not taste any of them.

text: Trevor's mother called him in the middle of class. He let it go to voicemail. She called again. He let it go. She texted him: "Have you seen the news?" He stepped out of the classroom. He took notes for the rest of the lecture. His handwriting was very small and very precise. After class, he walked to the registrar's office. The line was already out the door. He joined it. He stood in it for ninety minutes without complaint.

text: I had been treated for a condition I did not have. For two years. The doctor had been adjusting medications for a condition that was not mine. When I called the office to report the error, the receptionist put me on hold for twenty-six minutes. I sat with my phone on speaker, on the kitchen table, and I dismantled an old appliance with a screwdriver. Each screw I removed I lined up in a perfect row. By the time someone picked up, I had laid out forty-three screws. I told the woman my situation in a voice so calm she did not understand at first. I had to repeat myself. I repeated myself.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Erika opened the patient portal and found a procedure listed that she had not had. She had not had any procedure. She had been in for a routine physical. The portal listed a surgery from October. There was a surgeon's name. There was a recovery note. There was a billing line for forty-three thousand dollars. Erika did not panic. She did not call anyone yet. She took a screenshot of every page. She saved each one. She organized them in a folder on her desktop. She named the folder with the date. She closed the laptop. She walked to the kitchen. She drank a full glass of water without setting the glass down.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: The pharmacy had been giving me someone else's medication for six weeks. The dosage was double mine. The medication treated a condition I did not have. I figured it out when I read the new bottle's label and noticed a name that was not mine. The name was very similar. One letter different. I sat at my kitchen table with the bottle in my hand. I had not yet taken any pills from this bottle. I shook the bottle gently. I listened to it. I set it down. I picked it up. I set it down. I picked up the phone. I called the pharmacy. I waited on hold. I had time to wash all the dishes in the sink.

topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: Jamal was looking through his lab results when he noticed his date of birth was wrong. He was looking through someone else's results. He scrolled back through his portal history. The mixed records went back nearly a year. He had been making medical decisions based on these results. He had been worried about these results. topic: Someone discovers their medical records were mixed up with another patient's
text: I was a small breath away from a serious procedure I did not need. The pre-op nurse caught it. She caught it because of my allergy bracelet. She said, "Wait, this isn't your chart." They moved me to a different room. I sat up. I held the gown closed at the back. I asked who I needed to speak to. They said the patient relations office. I said thank you. I said it very politely.
